# Two papers, each written twice

Choose a PDF or find a study in the table below.

NeuroTranslation tests how much brain and muscle recordings add to forecasts that already use recent movement. It reports all 29 studies in the [numbered table](../benchmarks/README.md). Chapter 7 adds walking forecasts and a separate Next Neuron Prediction test on one rat recording.

**Brain2Body** proposes testing what a person retains after a machine stops guiding their hand through a tune. The paper proposes three ways to connect to a body (a pad on the brain, a strip along the spine, and a suit of fine gold electrodes that prick the skin), argues for trying them first in a small marsupial, and sets out the experiment and the results that would sink it. All three interfaces remain proposals. The paper reports no experiment on skill retention.

Each paper has a Technical edition, for readers who want the method, and a Simple English edition, which explains the same things in ordinary words and takes more pages to do it. Start with a Simple English edition.

| | Technical | Simple English |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *NeuroTranslation: A New Paradigm In Brain-Body Mapping.* | [PDF, 60 pages](current/neurotranslation-technical.pdf) | [PDF, 65 pages](current/neurotranslation-explained.pdf) |
| *Brain2Body: The Next Generation In Body-Brain Interfacing.* | [PDF, 29 pages](current/brain2body-article.pdf) | [PDF, 33 pages](current/brain2body-simple-english.pdf) |

[Read all four online](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/current/), or [download them in one ZIP](downloads/NeuroTranslation-Brain2Body-Papers.zip) and unpack the whole folder so that the links between its files work.

## Companion studies and demos

The reports below give results and source material for related studies and demos. Chapter 7 of NeuroTranslation gives the walking and one-rat spike comparisons in these editions.

### Forecasts from brain, muscle and movement: brain signals mostly made them worse

- **Earlier brain-cell firing and a rat's position a quarter of a second later.** A forecast from the rat's recent positions did worse when the firing of its brain cells was added. [The study](../benchmarks/wtrack-neural-motion/)
- **A recording from the surface of the brain, and five fingers.** One person bent the finger named on a screen while a glove measured all five and electrodes on the surface of the brain recorded. Once the recent glove readings and the screen were known, adding the brain recording made both fitted forecasts of the glove worse, a straight-line model and a small transformer (a kind of network that learns which earlier readings matter most); keeping the last reading did best (0.1774, against 0.2849 for the straight-line model with the brain recording). [The study, with the original study's ethics statement](../models/cortical-glove/README.md) · [Try invented inputs](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/finger-signals/)
- **Finger movement forecasts from a cue.** The same person and recordings as the item above, but no model is given a recent glove reading: given the finger named on the screen, a straight-line model and a small transformer both did better than with the brain recording added (0.288 against 0.354, and 0.289 against 0.321). [The study](../models/finger-motion/README.md) · [Try the six models](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/finger-motion/) · [The recorded brain-surface activity, by finger](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/Interoceptomics/recorded-cortex/)
- **Finger forecasts from cues and brain recordings.** A four-page note compares the three finger studies, from one person's later glove readings to five people each held out in turn. Tested on each person after learning from the other four, a table that knew only the finger on the screen and the time since it appeared did best on average (0.4770, against 0.5134 for a small transformer given the brain recording too); the right trial's brain recording did a little better than an earlier trial's. [HTML](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/finger-cues/) · [PDF](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/finger-cues/finger-cues.pdf) · [The cross-person study](../models/finger-transfer/)
- **Fingertip nerve activity as glass slides.** The study compares forecasts for three people left out of fitting, including what happens when the model sees force from a different slide. [Read the paper](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/touch-feedback/) · [PDF](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/touch-feedback/fingertip-touch.pdf)
- **Human fingertip recordings used to forecast macaque nerve activity.** A model trained on human fingertip nerves forecast the next 20 milliseconds of macaque activity. A simple forecast from the last 80 milliseconds of counts and the human training average scored better across the recorded macaque fibres. [Read the follow-up](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/touch-feedback/transfer/)
- **Recent spike counts forecast better in the gerbil recordings.** Models trained on human fingertip recordings forecast the next 20 milliseconds of auditory-nerve activity in 19 gerbils. A simpler average of recent counts scored better than both timing models. [Read the transfer test](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/touch-feedback/transfer/#auditory-transfer)
- **A two-page supplement on where the body goes next.** One experiment continues a measured human stride for 600 milliseconds; the other forecasts how far a rat will move in a quarter of a second from its movement and the firing of its brain cells. The walk or run label helped place body points measured from the hips (71.9 to 69.1 mm), and correctly timed firing improved on both comparisons in only one of three rats. [Read the supplement](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/forecasting-movement/) · [Download the two-page PDF](../docs/papers/forecasting-movement/movement-forecast.pdf) · [Editable source and figures](../docs/papers/forecasting-movement/)
- **A five-page supplement on treadmill walking.** The first experiment predicts where the knees will be 15 frames, about a quarter of a second, later: replaying a stride from four seconds of knee history (3.54°) beat a transformer that saw 0.4 seconds of the joints (4.46°). Given the same four seconds, a transformer trained to correct the replayed stride did better than both (2.679°); the general model's knee task was a little closer than the replay (3.465° against 3.535°, a difference within the noise), but no closer than the same correction without its shared part (3.460°); a copy with the shared part scrambled did better (3.422°), and the rule set in advance for a gain from the shared part failed. In a second laboratory, with ten walkers measured by cameras, that transformer beat the replayed stride for only six. The third asks whether leg-muscle and knee-angle recordings agree on a walking rhythm when the clocks cannot establish the timing of individual steps: the same walk's rhythms differed by 0.027 cycles per minute, another walker's by 3.055. [Read the supplement](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/walking-rhythm/) · [Download the PDF](../docs/papers/walking-rhythm/gait-clocks.pdf) · [Editable source and results](../docs/papers/walking-rhythm/) Its fifth page asks how well joint angles predict the knees' net turning moments, how hard the forces around each knee push it to bend or straighten: a copy of the general model's shared part trained for that task alone had the lowest average error of the methods that saw only angles (0.08874 newton-metres per kilogram of the walker's mass), though it beat the straight-line fit for two of three walkers and the walker match for one, failing the rule set before scoring, and copying an earlier measured moment did better where it was possible (0.06785). [The knee-moment task](../models/neurotranslate-0.0/load/)
- **One stride, two force plates.** A four-page supplement on two tests in slow overground walking, where eight electrodes on the right leg picked up its muscles as each walker crossed two force plates, panels in the floor that measure how hard a foot presses down. On 8 walkers kept out of fitting, adding the muscle signals made a forecast of the load on both plates worse (65.19 to 70.20 newtons). On the plate under the right foot, the general model did a little better with them (93.93 to 85.18), but a straight-line fit given the same signals did better still (82.04). [Read the paper](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/muscle-and-floor/) · [Download the PDF](../docs/papers/muscle-and-floor/muscle-and-floor.pdf) · [Inspect the fitted models](../models/walking-force/)
- **Wrist position a fifth of a second ahead.** A four-page supplement on two experiments in the same slow walking, both 200 milliseconds ahead on the stored recordings, both scored on ten walkers kept out of fitting, who had already been studied for other questions. Six markers on the skin, at both ankles, knees and wrists, followed together: a straight-line fit given the markers alone did best (17.78 mm on average), and the right leg's muscle signals changed a small transformer's error only within the noise (18.22 to 18.02 mm). And one marker at a time, the general model's single-marker task, tried at 46 places on the body it was not fitted on: a fit that compared each path with 64 stored training paths (28.73 mm) beat it (31.00 mm). [Read the study](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/walking-landmarks/) · [Download the PDF](../docs/papers/walking-landmarks/walking-landmarks.pdf) · [Try the six-marker viewer](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/walking-landmarks/)
- **Cued arm forecasts.** A four-page supplement on one person who saw a picture asking them to bend or straighten the supported right elbow, turn the palm up or down, close or open the hand, or rest. Its two experiments compare what the cue, the early readings of the arm's sensors and a scalp electrode add to a forecast of what the sensors measured later. Knowing the cue helped the general model (0.751 to 0.641; each error divided by how much that sensor's change at that horizon varied in the fitting runs), but the cue alone did better (0.525); adding scalp electrode C3 made the forecast of the elbow worse (0.07237 to 0.07859, in the sensor's own units). [Read the study](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/cued-arm/) · [Download the PDF](../docs/papers/cued-arm/cued-arm.pdf) · [Try an instruction](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/shared-motion/#cued-arm)
- **Forecasting cued arm movements in new people.** A four-page supplement on the same supported-arm task, with seven people supplying the examples and five others the test, opened, by the studies' own records, only after the models were fixed. On the five new people, the average change for each cue beat a small transformer trained for the task (0.467 against 0.493), and the training group's median change for each cue beat the general model fitted on the seven (0.435 against 0.505). It also asks what one practice run from a new person adds: a correction from that run lowered the general model's error on the person's later runs from 0.521 to 0.484, but simply predicting the person's own median change for each cue in that run did better (0.429), so the correction failed the rule set for it. [Read the study](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/arm-transfer/) · [Download the PDF](../docs/papers/arm-transfer/arm-transfer.pdf) · [Try the model](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/arm-transfer/)
- **Arm forecasts with and without early scalp readings.** A four-page illustrated supplement on the same task, scored on a fourth run of the five test participants that the plan required to stay closed until the models were frozen. It compares a forecast that knows the cue and the early movement with one that also sees six scalp electrodes or three around the eyes. Adding the scalp left a small transformer's error almost unchanged (0.50853 to 0.50856) and moved a straight-line correction fitted on top of the general model's unchanged shared part from 0.49777 to 0.49628, a difference within the noise that helped two of the five people; neither passed the test set in advance, and the usual change for each cue beat the transformer (0.49278). [Illustrated study](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/scalp-forecast/) · [Download the PDF](../docs/papers/scalp-forecast/scalp-forecast.pdf) · [Try the models](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/scalp-forecast/)
- **Neck-signal forecasts with and without an armpit recording.** A five-page illustrated supplement on people lying still while a nerve at the left wrist was stimulated again and again. From the readings up to 8 milliseconds after each pulse, two models forecast how far the voltage at the back of the neck 12 to 14 milliseconds after it will be from its level before the pulse; four people supplied the training data and six others the test. Carrying the last neck reading forward (8.09 µV on average) beat a small transformer (23.28 µV with the armpit's recording, 24.67 without it), and the armpit's recording passed neither model's test. [Illustrated study](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/cervical-forecast/) · [PDF](../docs/papers/cervical-forecast/cervical-forecast.pdf) · [Try the forecast](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/cervical-forecast/)
- **Back-sensor rotation a tenth of a second ahead.** A five-page illustrated supplement on people standing and walking with a sensor strapped to the back and two grids of electrodes on the skin over the spine. From the tenth of a second before, two models forecast how far the sensor would turn in the next tenth: a small transformer trained for the task and the general model. Both learned from four people; of the four kept for the test, one person's files could not be scored, so the planned test was never completed. On the other three, the electrodes made both forecasts worse (the transformer's error went from 0.361° to 0.382°, the general model's from 0.376° to 0.385°), and a straight-line fit on the turns alone did as well as the general model (0.376°). [Illustrated study](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/back-rotation/) · [PDF](../docs/papers/back-rotation/back-rotation.pdf) · [Try the forecast](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/back-rotation/)
- **Shin muscle-fibre length forecasts with and without fibre angle.** A five-page illustrated supplement on people pulling the foot upward while ultrasound filmed the muscle at the front of the shin and software tracked one bundle of its fibres. From the bundle's recent lengths, with or without its angles, two models forecast how much longer or shorter it would look ten tracking steps later: a small transformer trained for the task and the general model. Both learned from four people and were scored on four others, opened only after the models were fixed. The angles helped both a little (the transformer from 0.236 to 0.233 mm, the general model from 0.226 to 0.219 mm), not enough to pass the test set for them, and straight-line fits beat both (0.223 mm in the transformer's comparison, 0.215 mm in the general model's). [Illustrated study](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/muscle-tracking/) · [PDF](../docs/papers/muscle-tracking/muscle-tracking.pdf) · [Try the forecast](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/muscle-tracking/)
- **Movement forecasts with and without scalp recordings.** A ten-page illustrated follow-up to the wrist-and-sacrum study, scored only on its training people, eighteen on the beam and six lifting, each by models fitted on the others, with three different starting points for training. The joint transformer was given the voltages at three places on the scalp, against the same model given only the training group's averages there. The scalp's voltages made the wrist's path worse for all six lifting people (4.120 against 3.905 mm) and the sacrum's worse (2.699 against 2.667 mm), and the leg muscles' forecast a little better (11.370 against 11.385 µV), as much with another trial's voltages; holding each muscle's last strength did better still (11.355 µV). One of the four tests set in advance passed. [Read the study](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/cross-limb-movement/scalp-study/) · [Download the PDF](../docs/papers/cross-limb-movement/scalp-study/scalp-study.pdf) · [Paper source](../docs/papers/cross-limb-movement/scalp-study/scalp-study-source.zip) · [Try the scalp signals](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/cross-limb-movement/#scalp-input)
- **Shared and separate models for wrist and pelvis movement.** A seven-page illustrated follow-up to the wrist-and-sacrum study, scored only on its training people, eighteen on the beam and six lifting, each by models fitted on the others, with three different starting points for training. One version of the joint transformer turns what it has computed into a path with a separate last step for each body part, the other with one step of the same size that shifts its weight as the forecast runs on. The separate steps improved the pelvis path (2.582 against 2.645 mm) only as far as continuing the marker's speed over its last 31.25 milliseconds (2.583 mm), and left the wrist unchanged (3.878 and 3.877 mm); the test set for them failed. [Read the study](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/cross-limb-movement/decoder-study/) · [Download the PDF](../docs/papers/cross-limb-movement/decoder-study/decoder-study.pdf) · [Paper source](../docs/papers/cross-limb-movement/decoder-study/decoder-study-source.zip) · [Try the comparison](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/cross-limb-movement/#path-maps)
- **Movement forecasts for a point on an unfamiliar body.** Watch the model follow the points already visible. Change the shape of the figure, hide its future and compare the forecast with where the points actually land. [Read the study](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/first-use-body/) · [PDF](../docs/papers/first-use-body/first-use-body.pdf) · [Model and sources](../models/first-use-body/)

- **Next Neuron Prediction.** Add a spike to a fictional recording and see what happens to the forecast for every unit. The benchmark compares these probabilities with the next recorded spike. [Read the study](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/next-neuron-prediction/) · [PDF](../docs/papers/next-neuron-prediction/next-neuron-prediction.pdf) · [Model and sources](../models/next-neuron-prediction/)

- **Wrist forecasts tested on a different person.** An illustrated supplement of nine pages. On 30 left-wrist reaches by a person kept out of fitting, a regression trained on another person’s right-wrist reaches missed farther than continuing a fraction of the wrist’s earlier speed. The paper also compares a Transformer allowed to use both arms with the same architecture trained with attention between arms blocked. [Read the paper](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/cross-person-wrist/) · [PDF](../docs/papers/cross-person-wrist/cross-person-wrist.pdf) · [Editable source](../docs/papers/cross-person-wrist/cross-person-wrist-source.zip)
- **Next-day wrist forecasts with brain-surface voltage.** A supplement of nine illustrated pages on one person's arms, tracked by a camera, and eight of the electrodes on the surface of the brain: models fitted on 60 of the person's own reaches on one recording day forecast both wrists 8 and 15 camera frames ahead on 58 reaches of the next. Of the forecasts scored on all 58 reaches, no model beat the simplest (for the right wrist, its last position plus the training reaches' average movement; for the left, no movement). Against the same design fitted on positions alone, the voltages lowered the right-wrist error a little on the 57 reaches that had an earlier reach to lend its voltages, but another reach's voltages did as well or better in three of those six comparisons, and the test set in advance failed for both wrists. [Read the study](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/human-wrist/) · [Download the PDF](../docs/papers/human-wrist/human-wrist.pdf) · [Paper source](../docs/papers/human-wrist/human-wrist-source.zip) · [Try the forecast](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/human-wrist/)
- **Brain activity forecasts with arm movement added one week later.** A supplement of eleven illustrated pages on the reach-feedback models run, unchanged, on the same macaque seven days after they were fitted. Once another 100 milliseconds of the arm's movement had been measured, the spikes at 37 electrode contacts in area 2 over the 100 milliseconds after were predicted with and without it. Seeing the movement lowered the count error in one region of the apparatus (0.201) and raised it in the other (0.103), where predicting each contact's training average did better than both. Adding the spikes did not sharpen the forecast of the arm, and for 39 muscle–tendon paths calculated from the tracked arm, forecasting no change came closest. [Read the study](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/reach-feedback/one-week/) · [Download the PDF](../docs/papers/reach-feedback/one-week/one-week.pdf) · [Paper source](../docs/papers/reach-feedback/one-week/one-week-source.zip) · [Try the forecast](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/reach-feedback/one-week/)
- **Sensory-cortex forecasts using predicted arm movement.** A seven-page illustrated supplement on one macaque reaching to one target after another in two regions of an apparatus while electrodes in area 2 counted the spikes of 23 units. From 200 milliseconds of the arm's positions, the spikes and the go cues, one model forecast the next 100 milliseconds of movement, and a second used that forecast to predict each unit's spikes in the 100 milliseconds after. The forecast did not help: in the region the models were fitted in it raised the spike-count error by too little to tell from none (0.0035), and in the other region it raised it clearly (0.0100), where each unit's average count in the training reaches did better than either model. Earlier spikes brought the movement forecast closer to the hand there, but not to the elbow. [Read the study](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/reach-feedback/) · [Download the PDF](../docs/papers/reach-feedback/reach-feedback.pdf) · [Paper source](../docs/papers/reach-feedback/reach-feedback-source.zip) · [Try the forecast](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/reach-feedback/)
- **Forecasting how fast a cylinder turns.** A supplement of eight illustrated pages on people carrying a cylinder to one of nine targets while a sensor on top of it recorded how fast it turned and how it accelerated. From 200 milliseconds of those readings, the hand and the target, models forecast how fast it would turn over the next tenth of a second, on later trips by the same 24 people. Without the accelerometer the forecast was not clearly worse (0.1622 against 0.1584 radians per second), so the test set in advance failed; another trip's acceleration made it worse (0.1772), and the model did best without the target (0.1508). A separate test, on gestures repeated after a robot guessed wrong, found no help from naming the object. [Read the study](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/cylinder-rotation/) · [Download the PDF](../docs/papers/cylinder-rotation/cylinder-rotation.pdf) · [Paper source](../docs/papers/cylinder-rotation/cylinder-rotation-source.zip) · [Try the forecast](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/cylinder-rotation/)
- **Reach forecasts with and without the target.** A six-page supplement on people carrying a cylinder to one of nine targets shown on a screen: from 200 milliseconds of its tracked movement, the hand and the destination, models fitted on 24 people forecast where it would be, for seven others. On the planned clock, started at the first camera sample, the cylinder had barely moved and the test failed. Started once it had travelled 15 mm, a wrong destination made the forecast worse (17.79 mm against 12.13 mm at 0.6 seconds), but the right one did not clearly beat the movement alone (12.24 mm). A separate test, on gestures people improvised to show a named object, found no help from the name either. [Read the study](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/target-reach/) · [Download the PDF](../docs/papers/target-reach/target-reach.pdf) · [Paper source](../docs/papers/target-reach/target-reach-source.zip) · [Try another destination](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/target-reach/)
- **The same electrodes, one day later.** A five-page supplement on the macaque of the cortical-reach study, recorded on two days: models fitted on the first day's pushes forecast how many electrical events 26 contacts in area 2, a region of the brain that responds to touch and to the body's own movement, would record in the next 100 milliseconds of the second day. On 2,436 pushes, a small transformer did better with the right movement than with an earlier trial's (1.987 against 1.991, a count deviance, lower is better), but not clearly better than without the movement (1.990), so the test set for the movement failed, and a count regression given only the task's cues did best (1.905). [Read the study](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/contact-forecast/) · [Download the PDF](../docs/papers/contact-forecast/contact-forecast.pdf) · [Paper source](../docs/papers/contact-forecast/contact-forecast-source.zip) · [Try the forecast](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/contact-forecast/)
- **Reach forecasts with and without sensory-cortex recordings.** A seven-page illustrated supplement on one macaque's arm, pushed by a robot and then reaching for a target, with electrodes in area 2, a region of the brain that responds to touch and to the body's own movement. From the last 200 milliseconds, small transformers forecast how far the robot's handle would move in the next 100 milliseconds. On the day's last 108 trials, kept closed until the analysis was fixed, adding the spikes to the handle's movement and the task events made the forecast worse (0.6044 against 0.4974 cm), and spikes from another trial did no worse than the right ones. Two camera-tracked points on the hand and forearm helped a straight-line forecast during the push. [Read the study](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/cortical-reach/) · [Download the PDF](../docs/papers/cortical-reach/cortical-reach.pdf) · [Paper source](../docs/papers/cortical-reach/cortical-reach-source.zip) · [Try the forecast](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/cortical-reach/)
- **Sensory spike forecasts during muscle stretch.** A nine-page illustrated supplement on the muscle spindles of rats, the stretch sensors inside a muscle: a motor stretched the calf muscle while a sensor measured the pull on the tendon and an electrode recorded one sensory nerve fibre's spikes. From the last tenth of a second, models forecast how many spikes would come in the next 20 milliseconds. The planned test across three groups of the archive's files could not be run, so three fibres, all from one group, were scored in turn by models fitted on the other two. A small transformer given only the fibre's past spikes did best (0.446, a count deviance, lower is better); given the pull and position as well it did worse (0.499), so the test set for them failed, though swapping in the pull and position of a tenth of a second earlier made it worse still. Repeating the last count missed by the fewest spikes (0.325 on average). [Read the study](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/muscle-spindle/) · [Download the PDF](../docs/papers/muscle-spindle/muscle-spindle.pdf) · [Paper source](../docs/papers/muscle-spindle/muscle-spindle-source.zip) · [Try the forecast](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/muscle-spindle/)
- **Reach forecasts from a model trained on balance.** A six-page illustrated supplement on two datasets of different people: lifts after a light came on, with a tracker on the right wrist and electrodes over five muscles of the arm and hand, and standing or walking on a narrow beam while the view in a headset rotated, with a marker on the sacrum and electrodes over four muscles of each lower leg. From the last 0.625 seconds, one small transformer that learned both tasks forecast the marker's path and the muscles' signals over the next 125 milliseconds, against models that each learned one, from the same examples or for twice as many training steps. On nine people outside fitting, all scored before by earlier studies, the joint model was closer on the wrist than the wrist model trained on the same examples (4.870 against 5.100 mm) but not than the one trained twice as long (4.394 mm), and on the sacrum both balance models beat it (1.962 and 1.981 against 2.169 mm), so its test failed. [Read the study](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/cross-limb-movement/) · [Download the PDF](../docs/papers/cross-limb-movement/cross-limb-movement.pdf) · [Paper source](../docs/papers/cross-limb-movement/cross-limb-movement-source.zip) · [Try the model](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/cross-limb-movement/)
- **A shared model for leg-muscle activity and pelvis movement.** A six-page illustrated supplement on people standing on or walking along a narrow beam while the view in their headset rotated, with electrodes over four muscles of each lower leg and cameras on a marker at the base of the spine. From the last 0.625 seconds of both, one small transformer forecast how strong each muscle's signal would be and where the marker would go over the next 125 milliseconds, against two of the same kind that each forecast one. On six people outside the fitting group, whose walking an earlier study had already scored, forecasting the same sacrum marker 125 ms ahead, the two separate transformers were a little closer (9.45 µV and 1.940 mm, against 9.50 µV and 1.965 mm), so learning both together failed its test, and a straight-line fit did worse than both (10.70 µV and 2.12 mm). [Read the study](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/muscle-and-motion/) · [Download the PDF](../docs/papers/muscle-and-motion/muscle-and-motion.pdf) · [Paper sources](../docs/papers/muscle-and-motion/muscle-and-motion-source.zip) · [Try the model](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/muscle-and-motion/)
- **125-millisecond balance forecasts with and without scalp signals.** A six-page illustrated supplement on people walking a narrow beam while the view in their headset rotated, with cameras on the head and the base of the spine and electrodes on the scalp, beside the eyes and over muscles of the neck and legs. On six people opened only after the models were sealed, a small transformer forecast the next 125 milliseconds of both markers a little better without the scalp (7.668 against 7.798 mm at the sacrum), and a straight-line fit given only the movement and the rotation's direction beat both models (7.368 mm). [Illustrated study](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/visual-balance/) · [PDF](../docs/papers/visual-balance/visual-balance.pdf) · [Source of the supplement (ZIP)](../docs/papers/visual-balance/visual-balance-source.zip) · [Try the forecast](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/visual-balance/)
- **One footstep, two forecasts.** A six-page illustrated supplement on people walking barefoot across force plates while cameras tracked the right heel and the ball of the foot and eight electrodes picked up the right leg's muscles. From the same inputs, a small transformer forecast both where the heel marker would be and the upward force under that foot a tenth of a second later, against two transformers that each learned one; the general model forecast both as well. On eight people studied before, learning both at once gave a lead within the noise (1.156 against 1.183 mm, 92.36 against 93.73 newtons), and straight-line fits and carrying the plate's current reading forward did better. [Illustrated study](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/heel-and-force/) · [PDF](../docs/papers/heel-and-force/heel-and-force.pdf) · [Source of the supplement (ZIP)](../docs/papers/heel-and-force/heel-and-force-source.zip) · [Try the forecast](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/heel-and-force/)
- **Pedal load forecasts with a shin muscle signal.** A six-page illustrated supplement on people trying to lift a foot strapped to a pedal that could not move, while an electrode on the skin of the shin picked up the muscle's electrical activity and a sensor recorded the load on the pedal. From the last 201 readings of both, two models forecast the pedal's reading a tenth of a second later: a small transformer trained for the task and the general model. Both learned from two people; of the eight recordings kept from two others for the test, one could not be scored, so the planned test was never completed. The muscle signal helped the transformer for one test person (0.06257 to 0.05452) and hurt it for the other (0.12013 to 0.16696); the general model did best without it, ahead of a straight-line fit for both people (0.0434 against 0.0476 for the first), in a comparison with no pass mark set in advance; both had earlier given ultrasound recordings to its shin-muscle task. [Illustrated study](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/pedal-load/) · [PDF](../docs/papers/pedal-load/pedal-load.pdf) · [Try the forecast](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/pedal-load/)

### Words and movement: something simpler did about as well or better

- **An instructor's finished words and the wrist one second later.** Adding the words made the forecast of how far the wrist would move worse, and repeating its movement over the previous second did best. [The study](../benchmarks/preceding-instructions/)
- **A four-page supplement**, *How precisely do words identify a recorded movement?*, written to go with the NeuroTranslation paper but not part of it, reports the two studies that search recordings of movement with words, one of the whole body and one of the hand. It explains why the timing of an action can be easier to find than the shape of the hand, and which question about guiding a hand, the subject of the Brain2Body paper, the studies leave open. [Read it online](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/language-and-observed-movement/language-and-movement.html) · [Download the four-page PDF](../docs/papers/language-and-observed-movement/language-and-movement.pdf) · [Editable source and evidence](../docs/papers/language-and-observed-movement/)
- **Walking forecasts with a speed instruction.** A six-page illustrated supplement on people walking barefoot, told either "as usual" or "fast but not running". Both models forecast the next tenth of a second from 200 milliseconds of pelvis and right-heel motion. The comparison tests what the instruction adds. For a small transformer the help was within the noise (5.022 against 5.116 mm at the pelvis on ten people studied before), and the opposite instruction made it worse; the general model passed that test on the same ten people and failed it on the people it was fitted on. [Illustrated study](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/papers/walking-instructions/) · [PDF](../docs/papers/walking-instructions/walking-instructions.pdf) · [Source of the supplement (ZIP)](../docs/papers/walking-instructions/walking-instructions-source.zip) · [Try the forecast](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/walking-instructions/)
- **A stride from one word.** Enter **walk** or **run** and a small model generates a short stride from that word alone. On two walks and one run kept out of fitting, the average error of its body points was 89.82 mm, against 89.88 mm for the average recorded walk or run from training. [Generate a stride](https://eliminatenoise.github.io/NeuroTranslation/word-motion/) · [Recordings, method and results](../models/word-motion/)

### The general model, after its first fits: a model made for the wrist still did better

- **The general model's shared fit** learned a headset's tracking of people's wrists and a camera's tracking of a rat together; then, with that shared part left frozen, new input and output layers were fitted for a third task, the two angles of the wrist. Its forecast of those angles was later given a correction from four forearm signals, scored on six people the wrist studies had already used, each in turn by a version fitted on the other five: the error fell from 4.175° with a correction from the wrist's movement and the time since the cue to 4.054° with the forearm signals, and an earlier model made for the wrist still did better (3.549°). Given a rat's brain-cell firing beside its camera track, a readout fitted on its unchanged shared part lowered the distance error from 2.805 to 2.778 cm, but the firing passed both checks for only one of three previously scored rats, and a scrambled copy of the shared part did better (2.763 cm). [The model and its comparisons](../models/README.md) · [Comparison figure (PDF)](../models/figures/wrist-correction.pdf) · [Methods, paired comparisons and source](../models/neurotranslate-0.0/forearm/) · [The firing comparison](../models/neurotranslate-0.0/population/)
- **Nine more tasks, in the supplements above.** The general model's estimate of the force under the right foot, its single-marker task, its cued-arm task, with its shared part unchanged and its final readouts fitted on one person and then on seven, and its back-sensor, shin-muscle, pedal, heel-and-force, walking-instruction and visual-balance tasks are reported in the force-plate, walking-marker, arm-cue, arm-transfer, back-sensor, shin-muscle, pedal, heel-and-force, walking-instruction and visual-balance supplements. A simpler forecast beat it in all of them but three: on the back sensor a straight-line fit did as well; on the pedal it was closer than the simpler forecasts, from the pedal's own readings, in a comparison with no pass mark set in advance and an incomplete test whose two people had earlier given ultrasound recordings to the shin-muscle task, while the muscle signal made it worse; and with the walking instructions its average error was lower than theirs too, on people studied before, though a copy with its shared part left untrained did better (in the task's results; not in the supplement). [The right-foot task](../models/neurotranslate-0.0/right-plate/) · [The single-marker task](../models/neurotranslate-0.0/point-motion/) · [The cued-arm task](../models/neurotranslate-0.0/cued-arm/) · [The arm task across people](../models/neurotranslate-0.0/arm-transfer/) · [The back-sensor task](../models/neurotranslate-0.0/back_rotation/) · [The shin-muscle task](../models/neurotranslate-0.0/muscle_tracking/) · [The pedal task](../models/neurotranslate-0.0/pedal_load/) · [The heel-and-force task](../models/neurotranslate-0.0/heel_force/) · [The walking-instruction task](../models/neurotranslate-0.0/walking_cues/) · [The balance task](../models/neurotranslate-0.0/visual_balance/)

## Review status

These papers are working drafts. Project reviewers checked the results against their sources and read the current text for clarity. They have not been peer reviewed.

Where a paper and a result file disagree, the result file is right: [the studies page](../benchmarks/README.md) is written from the result files.

## The result files the papers name

Most studies keep their result file in their own folder under [`benchmarks/`](../benchmarks/README.md). The studies without a folder publish theirs here, beside the papers. The seven under `current/results/` hold aggregate numbers only, each with the file and field it was read from; the long training run's file is the run's own summary.

| File | What it holds | Where the papers use it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`link-macaque.json`](current/results/link-macaque.json) | One macaque: finger positions forecast from recordings in the part of the brain that drives movement, six recording days | NeuroTranslation, section 4.6 and appendix A |
| [`training-diagnostic-summary.json`](current/training-diagnostic-summary.json) | The long training run: one network fitted to a muscle signal and a glove's joint angles from one recording, against repeating the last value | NeuroTranslation, section 4.7 and appendix B |
| [`earlier-decoding.json`](current/results/earlier-decoding.json) | The earlier models that read the hand, the arm or the muscles from recorded brain cells, one recording at a time, and one tried on a different day | NeuroTranslation, sections 4.5 and 4.8, and appendix B |
| [`finger-intent-and-replay.json`](current/results/finger-intent-and-replay.json) | A model that read which finger a paralysed person was trying to move, on three later dates, and its choices replayed through a simulated hand | NeuroTranslation, section 4.8; Brain2Body, section 4.1 |
| [`simulated-arm.json`](current/results/simulated-arm.json) | A reach read from a macaque's brain cells, driven through a simulated human arm, and controllers rejected on a simulated macaque arm | NeuroTranslation, section 4.8 and appendix B |
| [`phrase-policy.json`](current/results/phrase-policy.json) | A simulated hand trained to play short phrases and chords at four keys, scored on phrases it had not been trained on | Brain2Body, section 4.2; NeuroTranslation, appendix B |
| [`muscle-pulse.json`](current/results/muscle-pulse.json) | One short pulse sent to one finger muscle of a simulated hand, against the same run without it | NeuroTranslation, section 7.3 |
| [`template-mesh.json`](current/results/template-mesh.json) | Faults found in one surface of the template brain | NeuroTranslation, appendix B |

## Source, checksums and licence

- **Source.** [One ZIP](downloads/NeuroTranslation-Brain2Body-Papers-Source.zip) holds everything that builds the four PDFs: the TeX of both papers, the bibliography, the figure, the seven font files and the tools (91 files in all), the build script, and the results every printed number is taken from. Its README names what it cannot include, the TeX engine and the package files the engine needs, and gives the command. Built from it with the same engine and the same 415 package files (the ZIP lists each by checksum), the four PDFs come out byte for byte the same as the ones here.
- **Checksums.** [`current.json`](current.json) names the edition and gives the checksum of each ZIP ([papers](downloads/NeuroTranslation-Brain2Body-Papers.zip.sha256), [source](downloads/NeuroTranslation-Brain2Body-Papers-Source.zip.sha256)). [`current/manifest.json`](current/manifest.json) gives the checksum and page count of each PDF, and the page of each study.
- **Licence.** The project's own text is dedicated to the public domain under CC0 1.0. The datasets, simulators and fonts the papers rely on keep their own terms, and [`current/NOTICE.md`](current/NOTICE.md) lists each with its credit. All dataset credits of the repository: [docs/RIGHTS.md](../docs/RIGHTS.md).

Each new edition replaces these files at the same addresses. Earlier editions are in the repository's history.
